title: The Seleucid Empire
description: An illustrated map of the Seleucid Empire, from Alexander’s death at Babylon and Seleucus’s return through the elephants of Ipsus, the founding of Antioch and the march of Antiochus the Great to Bactria, to Rome’s victory at Magnesia, the Maccabees, the Parthian conquest of Mesopotamia and Pompey’s end of the dynasty.
mapLabel: Illustrated map of the Seleucid Empire, from 323 BCE to today
note: Based mainly on Greek and Roman historians (Polybius, Diodorus, Appian, Justin and Josephus), the books of Maccabees, Babylonian tablets and excavated sites; each chapter says which it follows. Ancient army sizes and city populations are often too large. Dates for the breakaway of Bactria and Parthia are disputed. Bactra and the Indus lie beyond the map’s eastern edge, so routes run off the map towards them. Native names are given in Latin letters. The map is stylised and not to scale. Lands under Powers are painted loosely.

steps.title: Alexander dies at Babylon
steps.text: Alexander of Macedon dies at Babylon in June 323 BCE, aged 32, with no adult heir. His generals, the Successors (Diadochoi), agree to rule as governors in the name of his half-brother and infant son, then turn on each other. One officer present, Seleucus, commands the Companion cavalry; in 320 BCE he is made governor (satrap) of Babylonia.
steps.today: Today: the ruins of Babylon, near Hillah, Iraq; a World Heritage Site since 2019.

steps.title: Seleucus returns to Babylon
steps.text: Driven out of Babylonia by the general Antigonus in 316 BCE, Seleucus flees to Ptolemy in Egypt. After helping defeat Antigonus’s son Demetrius at Gaza in 312 BCE, he rides back to Babylon with a small force and is welcomed. Later dating counts its years from here: the Seleucid era, used across western Asia for centuries.
steps.today: Today: clay tablets from Babylon dated by the Seleucid era are in the British Museum and other collections.

steps.title: A new capital on the Tigris
steps.text: Seleucus founds Seleucia on the Tigris, where the Tigris and Euphrates run closest together, and makes it his eastern capital. Greek and Macedonian settlers live beside Babylonians. Pliny later says it had 600,000 people, a figure modern historians think too high, but it was among the largest cities of its age. In 305 BCE Seleucus takes the title king.
steps.today: Today: Tell Umar, about 35 km south of Baghdad, Iraq, across the Tigris from the ruins of Ctesiphon.

steps.title: Elephants from India win Ipsus
steps.text: Seleucus marches to the Indus, but Chandragupta Maurya is too strong. By a treaty, about 305 to 303 BCE, Seleucus gives up his easternmost lands for 500 war elephants and a marriage alliance; how much land changed hands is disputed. In 301 BCE, at Ipsus, his elephants cut off Demetrius’s cavalry and Antigonus is killed. Seleucus wins Syria.
steps.today: Today: Ipsus lay near Çayırbağ, in Afyonkarahisar province, Turkey; the exact battlefield is not known.

steps.title: Antioch on the Orontes
steps.text: Seleucus founds Antioch on the Orontes in 300 BCE, naming it after his father Antiochus. Nearby he founds Laodicea, after his mother, Apamea, after his wife, and Seleucia in Pieria, after himself, as Antioch’s port. Together they are the Syrian Tetrapolis (four cities). Antioch becomes the Seleucid capital and later one of the great cities of the Roman east.
steps.today: Today: Antakya, Turkey, badly damaged in the earthquakes of February 2023.

steps.title: Victory, then murder
steps.text: At Corupedium in western Anatolia, Seleucus, in his late seventies, defeats and kills Lysimachus, his last great rival, and wins Anatolia. He crosses into Europe to claim Macedon, his homeland, but near Lysimachia he is murdered by Ptolemy Keraunos, a son of Ptolemy I whom he had sheltered. His son Antiochus I inherits an empire from the Aegean to Iran.
steps.today: Today: Lysimachia lay near Bolayır, on the Gallipoli peninsula, Turkey.

steps.title: The east breaks away
steps.text: Far from Antioch, the eastern governors drift away. In Bactria (northern Afghanistan) Diodotus makes himself king, founding a Greek kingdom that lasts over a century. In Parthia, south-east of the Caspian, the governor Andragoras breaks away, and then the Parni, horsemen led by Arsaces, take the province, traditionally in about 238 BCE. Dates for both are disputed.
steps.today: Today: Old Nisa, near Ashgabat, Turkmenistan, an early Parthian royal fortress; a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: Elephant against elephant
steps.text: Antiochus III, king at eighteen, marches south to take Coele-Syria (the southern Levant) from Egypt. At Raphia, near Gaza, he meets Ptolemy IV; Polybius gives each side over 60,000 foot soldiers. His Indian elephants drive back Ptolemy’s smaller African ones and his right wing wins, but Antiochus chases too far, his centre gives way and he loses.
steps.today: Today: Rafah, on the border between the Gaza Strip and Egypt.

steps.title: The march to Bactria
steps.text: Antiochus sets out to win back the east. He makes Armenia and Parthia accept him as overlord, besieges the Bactrian king Euthydemus at Bactra for two years, then makes peace. He crosses the Hindu Kush and renews friendship with an Indian king, Sophagasenus, who gives him elephants. On his return he is hailed as “the Great”.
steps.today: Today: Hamadan, Iran. Bactra, beyond the map’s edge, is Balkh in northern Afghanistan.

steps.title: Panium wins the Levant
steps.text: Antiochus defeats Ptolemy V’s general Scopas at Panium, by the springs of the Jordan, in 200 BCE. Coele-Syria, with Judea and Jerusalem, passes from the Ptolemies to the Seleucids. Josephus records Antiochus confirming the Jews’ right to live by their own laws. Then he looks west, to Anatolia and Greece, where Rome is now the rising power.
steps.today: Today: Banias, in the Golan Heights, where a spring feeds the Jordan.

steps.title: Rome wins at Magnesia
steps.text: Beaten by Rome in Greece at Thermopylae in 191 BCE, Antiochus falls back. A Roman army under Lucius Scipio, advised by his brother Africanus, crosses the Hellespont and, with Pergamum, beats him at Magnesia. By the Treaty of Apamea (188 BCE) he gives up Anatolia beyond the Taurus, his elephants and his fleet, and pays a huge indemnity.
steps.today: Today: Manisa, Turkey. Apamea in Phrygia, where the treaty was made, is Dinar.

steps.title: The Maccabees rise
steps.text: Antiochus IV invades Egypt, but in 168 BCE a Roman envoy draws a circle round him in the sand and demands an answer before he steps out; he withdraws. In Jerusalem he backs Greek-minded priests, bans Jewish law and rededicates the Temple to Zeus in 167 BCE. The Maccabees revolt and retake the Temple in 164 BCE.
steps.today: Today: Jerusalem. Hanukkah, the festival of lights, still marks the rededication of the Temple.

steps.title: Parthia takes Mesopotamia
steps.text: The Parthian king Mithridates I takes Media and then, in about 141 BCE, Seleucia and Babylonia. The Seleucids lose their eastern heartland. Demetrius II, marching to win it back, is captured in 138 BCE. Antiochus VII tries again and is killed in Media in 129 BCE. The empire shrinks to Syria and Cilicia.
steps.today: Today: Tell Umar, south of Baghdad. The Parthians built their capital, Ctesiphon, across the river.

steps.title: Rome ends the dynasty
steps.text: Rival Seleucid princes fight each other for what is left. Tigranes the Great of Armenia rules Syria from about 83 to 69 BCE. When the Roman general Pompey comes east, he refuses to restore the dynasty and makes Syria a Roman province, in 64 or 63 BCE. The last Seleucid king, Antiochus XIII, is murdered soon after.
steps.today: Today: Antakya, Turkey, close to the Syrian border.

steps.title: Dura-Europos dug up
steps.text: Dura-Europos on the Euphrates was founded as a Seleucid fortress about 300 BCE, then held by Parthians and Romans until the Sasanians took it in about 256 CE. Sand buried it. Found in 1920 and dug by French and Yale teams, it has given up Greek records, a painted synagogue and one of the oldest known house churches.
steps.today: Today: near Salhiyah, Syria. Much of the site was looted during the Syrian civil war; its paintings are in Damascus and at Yale.

items.name: Seleucid Empire

facts.Capitals: Seleucia on the Tigris, then Antioch
facts.Ended: 64 or 63 BCE, when Pompey made Syria a Roman province
facts.Today: Iraq, Iran, Syria, Turkey and lands beyond

items.role: A successor state of Alexander’s empire, founded by Seleucus, which at its height stretched from the Aegean to Iran.

items.name: Antigonus’s realm
items.role: The lands of the general Antigonus, who drove Seleucus out of Babylonia and held Anatolia and Syria until Ipsus.

items.name: Ptolemaic Egypt

facts.Today: Egypt, Cyprus and, for a time, the southern Levant

items.role: The Greek dynasty founded by Ptolemy, which held Egypt and Cyprus and, for a time, Coele-Syria.

ties.text: Shelters Seleucus, then helps win Gaza

items.name: Parthia

facts.Capital: Ctesiphon, built across the Tigris from Seleucia

items.role: The Parni, horsemen led by Arsaces, who took a province from the Seleucids and came to rule Iran and Mesopotamia.

items.name: Rome and its allies
items.role: Rome and its allies in Anatolia, Pergamum first, then from 133 BCE the province of Asia, and after Pompey Syria and the Levant.

items.name: Seleucus I
items.text: A Macedonian officer who rose from cavalry commander to king of most of Alexander’s Asian empire. He founded dozens of cities, many named after his family. The marriage Alexander arranged for him at Susa in 324 BCE, to Apama, unlike most of those weddings, lasted. His surname Nicator means “victor”.

items.name: Apama
items.text: Apama was the daughter of Spitamenes, a Sogdian leader who had fought Alexander. She married Seleucus at the mass wedding at Susa in 324 BCE and was the mother of Antiochus I, so the dynasty was part Iranian from the start. Several cities named Apamea honoured her, the greatest on the Orontes in Syria.

items.name: Megasthenes
items.text: A Greek envoy whom Seleucus sent to Chandragupta’s court at Pataliputra. His book Indica is lost, but later writers such as Arrian and Strabo quote it: the seven classes of people, the city’s great wooden walls, the Indian elephant. Some of what he reported is exaggerated or second-hand.

items.name: Antiochus III
items.text: Antiochus III came to the throne at eighteen and spent his reign rebuilding his empire, east to Bactria and south to Gaza. He sheltered Hannibal, Rome’s old enemy, which helped draw him into war with Rome. After Apamea, short of money for the indemnity, he was killed in 187 BCE while plundering a temple in Elymais.

items.name: Antiochus IV
items.text: A son of Antiochus III, he spent years in Rome as a hostage after Apamea. As king he spent lavishly on Greek temples and games. Epiphanes means “god made manifest”; his enemies punned Epimanes, “the madman”. He died on campaign in Iran in 164 BCE.

items.name: Judas Maccabeus
items.text: Judas, called Maccabeus, “the hammer”, was a son of the priest Mattathias, who began the revolt. He led a guerrilla war against Seleucid armies and retook the Temple in 164 BCE. He was killed in battle in 160 BCE; his brothers fought on, and their family, the Hasmoneans, came to rule an independent Judea.
